name: Apathsahayar Temple, Thirupazhanam
deity: Shiva as Apathsahayar (Apatsahayeswarar), with the goddess Periyanayaki
period: Second shrine of the Saptha Sthanam of Thiruvaiyaru; a stone temple of the Chola king Aditya I, sung in the Tevaram (7th century)
dynasty: Chola (Aditya I), with later Nayak and Maratha patronage
summary: At Thirupazhanam, just east of Thiruvaiyaru, Shiva is worshipped as Apathsahayar, the helper in distress, in an early Chola temple that sends out its deities as the second stop of the Saptha Sthanam.

sections.history: Thirupazhanam lies on the northern side of the Kaveri a short way east of Thiruvaiyaru, and its temple is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams praised in the seventh-century Tevaram. The present stone shrine belongs to the reign of the Chola king Aditya I in the late ninth century. An inscription of his time on the south wall of the sanctum records twenty kalanju of gold given for a lamp that was never to go out, the gift of a lady related to the king's Pallava queen. Later records of Parantaka I, Rajaraja I and Kulothunga III follow, and the Thanjavur Nayaks and Marathas added contributions of their own.
sections.architecture: The temple is a compact early Chola work, singled out by scholars for the unusual plan of its vimana and of the ardhamandapa, the half-hall in front of the sanctum. The niche images on its walls have been coated in stucco over the centuries, softening their original lines. The goddess Periyanayaki has her own shrine in the outer enclosure, set apart from the lord's sanctum, and later mandapas and walls gather the whole into a quiet village temple.
sections.legends: The name Apathsahayar means the lord who comes to help in times of danger. Local tradition tells it through the story of Appar and his devotee Appoothi Adigal of neighbouring Thingalur, whose young son died of a snakebite on the very day the saint came to dine; Appar's prayer brought the boy back to life, and the lord of Thirupazhanam is remembered as the helper who answered. The sthala purana adds that Parvati is present beside Shiva in the sanctum itself, unseen.
sections.festivals: Thirupazhanam is the first temple the procession reaches after leaving Thiruvaiyaru in the Saptha Sthanam festival, held in the Tamil month of Chithirai (April–May). Tradition holds that the village, whose name speaks of fruit, sent fruits for Nandi's wedding, and its own deities set out in a glass palanquin to join the round. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are also kept. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thirupazhanam is a small, unhurried village, and the temple is best seen in the morning, when the old Chola walls can be studied at leisure. Look for the inscribed courses on the sanctum walls, then visit the goddess in her separate shrine. The temple pairs naturally with Thiruvaiyaru and Thingalur close by, and on the Saptha Sthanam night the village fills with pilgrims waiting for the palanquins.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but strictly prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Thirupazhanam is about 4 km east of Thiruvaiyaru on the road towards Kumbakonam, and roughly 15 km from Thanjavur. Local buses and autos run from Thiruvaiyaru. Thanjavur is the nearest major railway station, and Tiruchirappalli International Airport, around 65 km away, is the nearest airport.
